By Alexander Whiteman
28 October 2026
UK logistics groups welcomed the decision in today’s new budget to maintain a 5p-per-litre fuel duty cut and avoid planned increases, and ensuring warehouse rates do not rise, but there have also been warnings that businesses continue to face significant cost pressures.
In his first budget as chancellor – and first for the new Burnham government – John Healey rowed back plans to increase fuel duty by 3p per litre in January, followed by a further 2p rise in March, to ease some of the burden on the UK’s supply chains.
Logistics UK chief executive Ben Fletcher said the move was a “a wise decision” that would help keep trade moving, support economic growth and avoid adding to the already substantial inflationary pressures.
“We are delighted that that the Chancellor has listened to Logistics UK’s strong case for maintaining the duty cut at a time of global uncertainty and rising costs for businesses and consumers,” Mr Fletcher added.
Describing the price freeze as “the right call,” Road Haulage Association managing director Richard Smith said operators remained under severe financial pressure, citing the additional £385 per week hauliers were paying in fuel despite 85% reporting reduced margins.
Mr Smith said that the RHA has “been clear: a fuel duty hike is a food price hike, and with businesses and households struggling with additional fuel costs, the decision to keep prices frozen will offer some relief,” but stressed “ministers should have gone further”.
“The government can still support our sector as critical national infrastructure. A 15p per litre fuel duty rebate for essential users, similar to schemes elsewhere, would provide cashflow support, keeping many more haulage, coach and van operators in business,” he continued.
Elsewhere, the UK Warehousing Association (UKWA) welcomed the decision not to increase business rates on large warehouses, with chief executive Clare Bottle saying it was “a bullet dodged” after weeks of concern about higher property taxes.
“The UKWA has led the charge to persuade the government that a rise in property taxes for warehouses would inexorably lead to higher costs for business and consumers, and we are pleased our argument has been heeded,” she said.
However, Ms Bottle warned seven in 10 large distribution warehouses remained subject to the high-value business rates multiplier as operators faced rising fuel and employment costs, while also criticising policies that left businesses outside favoured sectors at a disadvantage.
Sharing the general view that the fuel duty freeze was a smart one, Metro Shipping offered a cautiously optimistic assessment, highlighting the more resilient growth forecasts and the removal of import tariffs on over 100 products.
In a statement, the company said that “whether the wider optimism translates into stronger trading conditions remains to be seen, but global container volumes are already setting new records”.

Volkswagen’s latest recall now extends to Audi, affecting nearly 13,000 Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally. And just like with the ID.4, owners are being told to limit charging to 80% of the battery’s capacity.
Volkswagen EV recall extends to Audi
Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs, model years 2023 to 2026.
Official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) revealed shortly after that several thousand more VW Group electric vehicles are affected worldwide.
In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, 72,668 VW Group EVs were included worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.
On October 27, VW Group added another electric vehicle to the KBA recall database. The latest recall impacts 12,734 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally, including just one in Germany. In total, Volkswagen’s battery recall now affects 85,402 EVs globally.
In the letter sent to the NHTSA on October 23, Volkswagen Group of America said it was issuing a recall affecting 9,048 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles in the US model years 2024 to 2025.
The recall stems from the risk of the battery overheating and potentially causing a fire under certain conditions when charged to over 80% of its limit.
Volkswagen said in a safety recall report with the NHTSA that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation.”
While the root cause is unknown, Volkswagen urged owners to limit charging to 80%. Owners of affected vehicles received an email saying VW “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%,” unless they opted out by October 21.
The safety recall follows Audi’s Product Safety Committee being informed of battery thermal events involving other Volkswagen Group EVs that use the same batteries as the Audi Q4 E-Tron.
Audi Q4 E-Tron (Source: Audi)
Following an internal investigation, Audi found the same battery and production characteristics as the impacted VW Group vehicles. Audi said the majority of these were produced for the North American market.
Audi is not aware of any claims, crashes, fires, injuries, or deaths associated with the Q4 E-Tron’s battery issue.

Tesla Semi Bursts into Flames, Fire Shuts Down California Highway
8 photos
Photo: KTVU FOX 2 San Francisco | YouTube
A Tesla Semi truck caught fire on an interstate in California, prompting a massive highway shutdown due to hazardous chemical smoke. It is the first known incident of its kind involving a Tesla Semi that combusted without being involved in a traffic collision.
The truck driver safely evacuated the vehicle before it was engulfed in flames. No injuries were reported, but the Semi was badly burned. Firefighters faced a fierce blaze that supposedly started in the vehicle’s high-capacity lithium-ion battery pack.
There is no information about the variant involved in the fire, but Tesla produces the Semi in two distinct flavors. The Long Range comes with the gigantic 822-kWh battery pack for a drive of up to 500 miles (805 kilometers) before it needs to be plugged in again, while the Standard Range is equipped with the 548-kWh battery pack, storing enough energy for a range of up to 325 miles (523 kilometers).
To put out the fire, the emergency response personnel deployed chemical foam, covering the tractor unit, while managing the risk of toxic airborne emissions. Firefighters successfully put out the fire faster than expected.
Photo: KTVU FOX 2 San Francisco | YouTube California Highway Patrol originally feared an 18-hour burn, similar to what they needed in the blaze that occured at the Frank Kent Cadillac dealership in Fort Worth, Texas, which took place back on October 9 and destroyed no fewer than six electric vehicles, all parked in the dealer's yard.
According to the official Tesla Semi Emergency Response Guide, first responders are strictly instructed never to submerge the vehicle to extinguish it. Instead, they must monitor the high-voltage battery temperature using thermal imaging cameras and store the vehicle at least 50 feet away from any structures for 24 hours after the fire is put out.
The fire broke out around 5:35 P.M. on Tuesday in the southbound lanes of the I-880 near Route 92. The California Highway Patrol (CHP) completely closed both directions of the freeway by 5:45 P.M. Northbound lanes reopened at 8:40 P.M., while the southbound lanes remained blocked for nearly ten hours, fully reopening around 3:30 A.M. on Wednesday.
The cause remains under investigation. The driver told the California Highway Patrol officers that the big rig " simply caught fire ," and he had no idea what triggered it, which points to a potential internal electrical or thermal fault in the high-voltage battery pack. The spontaneous combustion draws fresh scrutiny from the federal regulators.
Photo: CHP Hayward | X The incident follows a previous Tesla Semi fire in August 2024 near Emigrant Gap on Interstate 80. However, back then, the Semi caught fire after it went off the road and hit a tree, requiring 50,000 gallons of water and aerial fire retardant to cool down.
The incident is bad timing for Tesla. The firm has recently sent the Semi into production at the factory in Sparks, Nevada, just outside Reno, after multiple delays. WASHINGTON — The US, United Kingdom and Australia wrapped up a naval exercise this month that the Royal Navy billed as the three countries’ “largest ever demonstration of uncrewed and autonomous technology” in support of AUKUS Pillar II .
During the Maritime Big Play exercise, the AUKUS partners tested autonomous systems off the coast of San Diego, California, and integrated them into maritime operations — including tracking underwater threats and sharing data across platforms. The exercise comes as the UK and other European countries look to expand their maritime surveillance capabilities with autonomous systems amid growing security concerns in the region.
The UK headed up the anti-submarine warfare (ASW) portion of the exercise, using “a range of uncrewed surface vessels, underwater gliders, drones and subsea vehicles” during the exercise, according to a Royal Navy news release. Specifically, the ASW component focused on using both manned and unmanned systems for tracking and surveillance missions.
Altogether, the exercise was designed to showcase more than 40 technologies from the three AUKUS countries — including manned, unmanned and “multi-domain autonomous” systems, the release said.
The Royal Navy did not respond to a request for comment regarding how many and which types of unmanned systems were used in the exercise. The US Navy said in a news release that the drill’s ultimate goal was to “achieve milestones in integrating mature robotics and autonomous systems within AUKUS coalition maritime operations.”
The three countries established the AUKUS framework in 2021, with Pillar I focused on providing Australia with Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines by 2032. Under Pillar II of the deal, the nations are working together to jointly develop and field advanced military capabilities.
“Maritime Big Play demonstrates the real, tangible progress we are making with our AUKUS partners to deliver cutting-edge autonomous capability at sea,” Second Sea Lord Vice Adm. Paul Beattie said in a statement this month. “This is about more than technology on display, it’s about proving that our forces can operate together seamlessly, sharing data and combining assets to stay ahead of future threats.”
European nations are broadly pursuing maritime surveillance capabilities, with different priorities depending on each country’s geographic location and security concerns — from monitoring Russia’s activity in northern waters to tracking the flow of people through the Mediterranean in the south.
““As a result, countries are buying small numbers of manned patrol platforms and combining them with uncrewed aircraft,” Bryan Clark, director of the Hudson Institute’s Center for Defense Concepts and Technologies, told Breaking Defense . “In the south, they tend to want uncrewed aircraft plus manned patrol ships to intercept migrants. In the north, countries are buying manned ASW patrol aircraft like the P-8A [Poseidon] or Atlantique, plus uncrewed aircraft like the MQ-9B [SkyGuardian] .”
Zak Schneider, a visiting fellow at the Casimir Pulaski Foundation in Warsaw, also noted that maritime surveillance platforms have become critical capabilities for monitoring Russia’s escalation in the European theater.
“Sensors, ISR, intel and other data feeds are vital to being able to act on/forecast in advance new attacks in the maritime domain,” Schneider told Breaking Defense. “So, surveillance is also about the proliferation of sensors, detectors and reconnaissance that can feed data into these big systems. “
As European allies look for better ways to detect and track underwater threats, the AUKUS partners are also pursuing new sensor technologies for uncrewed systems. To cap off the Maritime Big Play exercise, the UK’s Ministry of Defence announced Tuesday that the country would spearhead d evelopment of three advanced undersea sensor payloads for unmanned systems, which the ministry said would become “available” to the UK, Australia and the US in 2027, in support of the AUKUS agreement.
The sensor payloads consist of a synthetic aperture sonar, a deployable anti-submarine warfare sensor and a deployable non-kinetic effector. The systems will be designed to conduct surveillance, collect underwater information and dispatch sensors that can track and identify underwater threats, according to the Ministry of Defence.
“The UK is all in on AUKUS, and this cutting-edge technology shows why,” UK Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard said Tuesday in a statement. “By leading development of these sensor payloads, we’re putting British innovation at the heart of AUKUS and strengthening our collective undersea capability.”

About 250 union watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach could strike as early as 5 p.m. Pacific time Sunday, Nov. 1, threatening cargo operations at the nation’s busiest container port complex if negotiators fail to reach a new labor agreement.
Members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 have authorized a strike, according to the Pacific Maritime Association, which represents employers. The employers group said negotiations are continuing with the assistance of federal mediators.
The potential disruption could extend well beyond the security workforce. PMA said the watchmen represent about 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports, but work at terminals handling roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo. The employer group expects other ILWU members would honor picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected facilities.
The watchmen’s previous agreement expired in July 2025, and employees have continued working under extensions. The latest extension expires Sunday, following more than a year of negotiations that have left the union and employers divided.
PMA said significant differences remain but pledged to keep negotiating.
“The Pacific Maritime Association remains committed to reaching a fair agreement with ILWU Local 26 at the bargaining table, and we will continue to negotiate in good faith through the November 1 deadline and beyond if necessary,” the association said in an email to FreightWaves.
Employers said their offer includes wage increases and pension improvements. The local has not detailed its demands. The PMA said full-time watchmen currently earn an average of more than $170,000 annually, plus fully employer-paid health care and pension benefits.
The contract of Local 26 members is separate from the coastwide agreement covering ILWU longshore workers and marine clerks, which runs through 2028.
The strike threat comes as the LA–Long Beach complex is already contending with a backlog of containers awaiting inland rail transportation. Terminal congestion and difficulties positioning enough rail equipment in Southern California have contributed to delays, raising concerns about the movement of holiday merchandise toward the eastern United States.
Why it matters: A strike by just 250 watchmen could become a much larger cargo shutdown if other union dockworkers honor the local’s picket lines.

Less-than-truckload carrier Old Dominion Freight Line saw tonnage turn positive for the first time in over two years during September. Executives from the company cited favorable market share opportunities on Wednesday, with customers exploring multiyear contracts and 3PLs seeking long-term capacity commitments. However, the company acknowledged that a more material demand inflection—requiring a resolution to record energy prices—will be needed to drive upcycle-like results.
Old Dominion ( NASDAQ: ODFL ) reported third-quarter earnings per share of $1.65 ahead of the market open on Wednesday. The result was 4 cents better than the consensus estimate and 37 cents higher year over year.
Revenue of $1.59 billion was 13% higher y/y (up 5% y/y excluding fuel surcharges) and $20 million better than analysts’ expectations. (Diesel prices were 48% higher y/y during the quarter.)
Table: Old Dominion’s key performance indicators
Tonnage per day was flat y/y, with a 13% increase in yield (revenue per hundredweight) driving the topline increase. Yield was up 5% y/y (ex-fuel), slightly better than management’s guidance (plus-4% to plus-4.5%).
The tonnage result was driven by a 2% y/y decline in shipments, which was offset by a 2% increase in weight per shipment. Tonnage was down roughly 1% y/y in both July and August, but up 1.6% in September and into October. The carrier continues to face easy prior-year comps (tonnage was down 10.7% y/y in the 2025 fourth quarter).
August updates from public carriers showed y/y tonnage growth has continued to accelerate cumulatively since first turning positive in March. September marked a ninth straight month of expansion for the manufacturing complex, and the LTL industry is seeing some freight return that was previously lost to a depressed truckload market.
Old Dominion is carrying over 35% excess door space currently, but noted that it should meaningfully take market share as capacity-constrained carriers are experiencing service failures. Old Dominion normally outgrows the market by 9 to 10 percentage points in an upcycle.
Higher shipment weights were a modest drag on the yield metric, partially offset by a slight increase in length of haul. Revenue per shipment (ex-fuel) increased 7% y/y. Old Dominion implemented a 4.9% general rate increase on Oct. 5.
A 71.5% operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ) was 280 basis points better y/y and 40 bps better than the midpoint of management’s guidance range (150 to 200 bps of sequential deterioration from the 70.1% second-quarter unadjusted OR). Shipments per employee (per day) were 2% higher y/y. Revenue per shipment (including fuel surcharges) was up 15.5% y/y, with cost per shipment up 11%—a 440-bp favorable spread.
October trends, Q4 guidance
October revenue per day is 22% higher y/y given a modest tonnage increase and a roughly 20% jump in yield (up 5.5% to 6% ex-fuel). Yields continue to accelerate, even with the added headwind of higher shipment weights (up 3% y/y in October).
Management pegged fourth-quarter revenue to a range of $1.54 billion to $1.58 billion, implying better-than-normal seasonality and coming in ahead of the $1.51-billion consensus estimate.
The carrier normally sees 200 to 250 bps of sequential OR degradation from the third to the fourth quarter. It expects to perform at the better-end of that range this year, implying a fourth-quarter OR of 73.5%, which would be 320 bps better y/y.
It said an annual insurance true-up could swing the number 20 bps either way. It also flagged higher healthcare costs and fuel (operating supplies) as potential headwinds. However, demand is holding steady (third-quarter shipments and tonnage slightly outpaced seasonality), and yield is outperforming.
The fourth-quarter OR outlook implies a 43% incremental margin versus 50% in the third quarter.
Shares of ODFL were down 5.5% at noon on Wednesday compared to the S&P 500, which was up 0.2%.
Investors are concerned that an inflationary diesel fuel environment is allowing LTL carriers to over-earn and that results will likely moderate when prices recede. There’s also some concern around industry growth prospects even after a positive inflection in manufacturing data.
Why it matters? Old Dominion Freight Line’s third-quarter report serves as a key industry bellwether, signaling that LTL carriers are successfully prioritizing pricing discipline and profitability over volume despite only modest demand trends.

Analysts hailed the Phase 3 head and neck cancer results as a big victory for an asset central to Genmab’s growth plans.
A late-stage trial of Genmab’s petosemtamab hit its co-primary endpoints at the first interim analysis, the biotech said Wednesday, completing a clean sweep of victories in a high-stakes run of readouts.
The LiGeR-HN1 study tested petosemtamab, a bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and LGR5, in combination with Merck’s Keytruda in nearly 700 patients with PD-L1-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Given as a first-line treatment, the combination significantly improved overall survival (OS) and objective response rate (ORR) compared to single-agent Keytruda, meeting its co-primary endpoints.
The investigational combination reduced the risk of death by 50%, regardless of HPV status.
William Blair analysts in a Wednesday morning note called the result “exceedingly positive,” while their counterparts at Truist Securities hailed the OS finding as “highly compelling and potentially practice-changing.”
Genmab has now delivered positive data on three key candidates in quick succession. At the start of October, the biotech was preparing to share Phase 3 data on its AbbVie-partnered bispecific antibody Epkinly, the antibody-drug conjugate rinatabart sesutecan (Rina-S) and petosemtamab. Weeks later, Genmab has positive data from all three studies.
Genmab’s stock rose 29% to $57.57 in early trading on Wednesday.
“We view the Rina-S and peto OS wins as particularly striking and believe all three franchises can support multibillion-dollar opportunities,” Truist analysts said. “Full data remain important given the first interim analysis, and we look for additional color on OS maturity, absolute ORR, safety and regulatory timing.”
Genmab has yet to disclose the median OS or ORR. Based on Keytruda’s historical performance in the setting, Truist analysts estimate that the petosemtamab combination may have achieved a median OS of about 30 months, broadly in line with the 28.2-month result seen in Phase 2. The analysts forecast that the ORR result could be in the 44% to 58% range.
The earlier-than-expected interim OS hit could accelerate Genmab’s path to market, Truist said. Analysts had initially expected OS results in 2027.
The OS success suggests “a particularly strong treatment effect” and supports potential approval in 2027, Truist said—ahead of the 2028 approval currently modeled by Truist. Bringing petosemtamab to market earlier than expected would give Genmab more time to grow sales of the product before the expiration of patents on Darzalex, its Johnson and Johnson-partnered multiple myeloma drug.
Preparing for the patent loss, Genmab invested in Epkinly, an internally discovered program, and struck deals for petosemtamab and Rina-S. Petosemtamab represented the biggest bet, with Genmab acquiring the drug candidate in its $8 billion takeover of Merus in September 2025.

U.S. Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, delivers a speech during the keynote session of TechNet Indo-Pacific 2026 at the Hilton Hawaiian Village, Honolulu, Hawaii, Oct. 27, 2026. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Daniela Lechuga Liggio)
WASHINGTON — Electronic systems used by US and allied forces are jammed daily on the Korean Peninsula, making it one of the most “violently contested electromagnetic environments on the planet,” according to a top US commander.
“Our adversaries practice electronic attack daily. They jam GPS in the West Sea. They attempt to blind our servers, our sensors, and our networks,” Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of US Forces Korea, said Tuesday during a presentation at AFCEA TechNet Indo-Pacific in Hawaii.
While Brunson did not specifically name an adversary nation, he noted earlier in his remarks that “across the demilitarized zone” US forces face a “nuclear-armed adversary that constitutionally designates the Republic of Korea as its principal enemy” — a reference to North Korea. China is also known to have advanced electronic attack capabilities in the region.
To operate in this complicated environment, Brunson said forces must have resilient and redundant capabilities.
“If your capability requires pristine satellite communications, infinite bandwidth, and uninterrupted fiber optic backbone to function, it will not survive 48 hours on the peninsula,” Brunson said to the audience consisting largely of industry members.
He noted that USFK is fielding resilient high-frequency networks alongside proliferated low-Earth orbit satellite communications and terrestrial mesh networks to maintain command and control when primary comms links are disrupted.
Brunson implored the industrial base to visit the peninsula to see the dynamic environment first hand. But, for industry members making the trip, he said they need to bring lightweight, jam-resistant waveforms with low probability of intercept and low probability of detection. He also asked industry to produce Open Application Programming Interfaces and edge sensors that can integrate with joint mission networks without vendor lock-in.
Although officials have emphasized joint and coalition interoperability for years, Brunson noted that industry must start designing systems to work with partner nations from the start.
“We can no longer design exquisite systems for pure US enclaves and then try to bolt on partner interface after the contract is signed. We must design combined from the first line of code,” he said. “To get there, we have to change a fundamental security mindset.”
For over 30 years, the mindset was to build security around hardened pipes and perimeter defenses in closed networks with stringent classification, he said. When information needed to be shared with partner nations, that approach required building a new pipe.
“In a combined fight inside the weapons engagement zone, that model has failed. Hardened pipes isolate our formations. They create operational blindness,” he said. “We must shift from network-centric perimeters to data-centric security. Tag the payload and not the pipe.”
In practice, a Korean radar detecting an inbound missile would have its track verified, ingested and pushed to coalition fires network in milliseconds, Brunson said. He stressed that information must move in milliseconds — not seconds.
Turning Industry Into ‘Pickle Millionaires’
Brunson urged the audience of industry players to pay close attention to the Pentagon’s direction and strategic documents to find what the military needs and provide it, likening industry’s North Star to pickles.
Brunson said the company Vlasic became “pickle millionaires” by recognizing that consumers needed sliced pickles — not whole ones — for their burgers.
“If you continue on a course that says, ‘Hey, man, we only do one thing, we do pickles and brine, that’s us,’ then you would never get pickles on a burger,” he said. “Pickles are long. You don’t put a pickle spear on a burger. You put those little sliced pickles on there.”
In the same vein, he urged industry to adapt its offerings to meet military requirements rather than trying to force products that don’t fit.
“The instructive part of this is, industry’s got to do the same thing. What is your sliced pickle? And if it doesn’t fit with where someone’s going, you cannot try to force it in there,” he said. “If a service tells you who they are and what they’re going to do and you choose not to try to meet the requirements of how they’re going to fight, that’s going to be a problem.”
He pointed to the Army’s recently released “How the Army Fights,” a strategic document outlining its operational guidance as an example of how companies can align their products with the service’s needs.
Brunson warned that networks will be under attack in the future as forces operate in increasingly disaggregated and distributed ways, with plans potentially changing before forces even arrive in theater. Capabilities that cannot adapt to that requirement will struggle to support the Army’s approach to warfare, he added.
“If your product can’t operate on the edge, then it’s not a product that’s going to be able to help the Army fight the way the Army is going to fight, much less the joint force,” Brunson said.

BougeRV Dropped Their New Diesel Heater and It's Already Tearing Up the Review Boards – Just $200
17 photos
Photo: BougeRV
With winter literally knocking on the Northern Hemisphere’s door, it’s time for RV and camper owners to start gearing up with the heating solutions they’ll be calling upon to stay warm, and one of the freshest is BougeRV’s latest portable diesel heater for outdoor use.
Diesel heaters are often called-upon in the RV and camping world, so BougeRV, a brand known to taper to the outdoor enthusiast, has unveiled their latest option, one that, for the time being, is selling for no more than $200, so clearly, an tool to be on your menu. Let’s see what’s in store here.
Now, what we’re looking at here is an outdoor heater, one that requires us to mount it externally or leave it outside overnight as it heats the interior of whatever it is we’re trying to make comfortable. That can be an RV, a camper, travel trailer, tent, annexes, and more.
Photo: BougeRV Before going on, allow me to point out one thing. This heating option has been around since September 2026, and nearly two months later, over 80 people have decided to step up to the plate and leave a review for their experience with this trinket. In all, it carries a 4.8-star rating out of five, making it one of the hottest, literally, heaters on the market right now.
One big reason why is that it can heat a space with over 300 cubic feet (8.5 cubic meter) of space in as little as 8 minutes. Keep in mind that test settings started out with the tent holding true to a nice freezing 32 degrees Fahrenheit (0 Celsius) inside, and after those eight minutes, it was a toasty 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20 Celsus). Let that thing run a bit longer, and you may need to sleep in your underwear. Five kilowatts (BTU) are pumped out by the system .
Another big win for the heater is the setup time, which, according to Bouge, takes just one minute. In three steps, which include attaching the muffler and pulling in the exhaust pipe, you’re set and heating up wherever you are. Well, as long as you have a power supply or the 12 V adapter with you.
Photo: BougeRV Keep in mind that another section of the product page does mention setup taking as much as 2 minutes. No matter what, people don’t seem to mind. This quick setup also means that you won’t have to bear the cold for too long, which is essential and a clock that starts ticking the moment that you step out of your truck or 4x4.
More on the design side of things, Bouge crafted this heater to be as easy to maneuvers possible, with the system weighing 22 lbs (10 kg). It’s also around 15 inches (38.1 cm) long, under 10 inches (25.4 cm) wide, and a bit over 12 inches (30.5 cm) tall. Two grab handles and an LCD display are also in place.
I do need to point out that Bouge created this solution to also be as clean as possible, and aside from the “leakproof” design with “automotive” gas cap, the unit can operate at under 70 decibels (65 dB in the video).
According to the clip below, the fuel consumption on this thing is pretty amazing too, able to burn as little as 0.18 liters per hour, or 0.0476 gallons.
Photo: BougeRV According to the manufacturer, this efficiency is good enough for as much as three nights or a peak of 27 hours of runtime. Hot damn! With the way fuel prices are looking these days, more power to you Bouge, more power to YOU.
Now, a heating system flowing through the night, which literally taps into burning a fuel, may make you feel uneasy as you catch those Zs. But, to remove any doubts from your mind that the heater will go up in flames in the middle of the night, BougeRV includes five layers of safety.
One of them is overheating, clearly, but then we also have over-voltage, the leakproof goodness I mentioned, short circuit, and reverse connection protection. Basically, there’s no way you can get it wrong.
Photo: BougeRV The last component that we have on the menu of closeups is the LCD display and control panel. It's from this side-mounted piece of gear that we’ll manage our heating output and keep tabs on diagnostics.
There is also a timer and a schedule function that you can play around with, so if you are out there and coming back late, your tent will heat up just five minutes before you arrive, if you want it to. App control is also pat of the goodies and so are a rain cover and carrying case.
Now, BougeRV took this system and tested it at an altitude of nearly 10,000 ft, 9,842 ft (3,000 m), to be precise, and they pledged that this thing still worked just fine. Frankly, I'm starting to understand why so many people have said yes to this rather new solution already, and if I may, I too am interested in giving it a try. I’ll try and get in touch with Bouge to try and get my hands on a test unit. Maybe it’s as good as they say.

Meet the Kia PV5 electric campervan
The PV5, Kia’s first 100% electric van, has been a huge success for the Korean automaker. After launching it at the end of last year, the PV5 has already become Europe’s top-selling small (C-segment) electric van.
Based on its modular skateboard platform, called E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to build custom configurations.
Although the PV5 is primarily sold in Passenger for everyday driving and Cargo for business use, Kia said the platform unlocks “endless possibilities” for different body styles and conversions, including a full-on electric campervan.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Wellhouse Leisure, a family-run campervan manufacturer based in the UK, revealed the Kia PV5 i-Camper.
The fully electric campervan is “now built and ready to view,” the company said. Based on the PV5 Cargo Plus, the campervan measures 4.69 m long, 1.89 m wide, and 1.99 m tall, which is about the size of a Ford Custom.
Although that’s pretty small for a camper, it offers more than you’d expect. Inside, the PV5 i-Camper includes two double beds with an elevating roof, a full kitchen setup, and a 200 W solar panel.
The sliding seat system enables the two rear seats to fold flat to form a bed and can be removed entirely. The upper bed, under the pop-up roof, has “more comfy” Froli Springs.
In the kitchen, you’ll find a sink with a tap and an electric water pump, two induction burners, a 42 L refrigerator, cabinets and storage spaces, and an optional microwave.
The vehicle also has a lithium leisure battery and a 12V supply, so you don’t need to use the vehicle’s main battery while camping.
It also comes with vehicle-to-load, letting you power external electrical devices, an e-bike, or even a campsite.
The PV5 Plus Long Range model uses a 71.2 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 247 miles. However, the added equipment will impact the range in the campervan conversion. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes using a DC fast charger.

This Hardshell Sidecar Camper Hooks Up to Torque-Loving Motorcycles To Give Us a Home Away From Home
9 photos
Photo: Sidewinder Sidecar Campers
I recently stumbled across a camping solution, and while that’s nothing out of the ordinary for me, what is special about the Mojave is that it’s aimed at motorcycle owners, and oddly enough, mounted in a sidecar position.
That’s right folks, the Mojave is a camper that’s aimed at motorcycle owners, and while campers for this type of vehicle do exist, this is the first one that I've ever seen that places the habitat at the side of the bike, and not behind it.
Now, the Mojave may seem familiar, especially if we consider that it’s just the biggest version of another unit that I shed light on recently. The Pygmy is that camper, and the Mojave is simply the largest layout from Sidewinder, the team responsible for the RV here today.
Photo: Sidewinder Sidecar Campers Come to find out, Sidewinder Sidecar Campers is a very new crew, having been established in 2025, making them a pup when compared to other brands that still produce motorcycle campers. But, as you’re about to find out, Sidewinder does things very differently.
One of the stand-apart features of the Mojave is that it’s a hardshell solution, and with the right heating systems, two people can take this one well into the colder months. The walls are also insulated and a layer of composite with weather coating makes up the exterior.
A benefit of making a camper this small and using composite to complete it is that you can use entire panels, uninterrupted by seams and joints that can leak, and by the looks of things, that’s precisely what Sidewinder has done here. Each sidewall is one piece, along with the roof, and the rear hatch over the galley at the rear.
What can still leak, as is true for any camper or RV, are the seams around windows, doors, the rear galley, and roof-mounted AC units. Be sure to stay on top of upkeep, as you should with any glamping solution .
Photo: Sidewinder Sidecar Campers As you’d expect that shell is set upon a steel chassis that is then connected to your bike via a custom system that Sidewinder has created for the purpose of staying in control as you ride around with this thing attached to just two wheels; the Mojave brings the third wheel.
According to Sidewinder, the Mojave is created for longer trips out there, with more storage, a larger interior, and the ability to accommodate more systems, all in the name of keeping you on the road for as long as you wish.
As we can see, the Mojave can be equipped with an AC unit on top, roof racks, solar panels – clearly, a battery is hiding somewhere, and it is – side-mounted shower, the possibility to add an annex, and countless others. An awning also means that we can set up a dining area too.
Like any camper of this size and style , the Mojave is rocking a rear kitchen, one accessed by lifting the rear hatch, as is traditional of teardrop campers. It’s here that we’ll cook our meals with the help of a cooktop (optional), sink, and fridge with slideout, and hide all our foodstuffs in their own allotted place. Don’t forget that the rear hatch also acts as a cover while you cook.
Photo: Sidewinder Sidecar Campers As for the interior of these bad boys, they aren’t the most decked out, as you’d expect of a space so small, but we do have features like lighting, the heating or cooling, windows integrated into the shell, somewhat of a skylight, and a modular mattress system you can stack to make a bit of a crash pad. What else do we need honestly?
What I found rather neat about the interior isn’t that it can handle the lifestyle of two people, but rather, that it can still carry a person inside while you’re on the move. It’s a trait that your average motorcycle trailer can’t achieve. Some custom ones can, but there are few out there. I’ve added images of some options that came before these sidecar RVs.
In its lightest form, the Mojave comes in with a dry weight of as much as 550 lbs (250 kg), so clearly, you’ll need a decently strong bike to move this turtle shell with wheels. According to Sidewinder, their products are designed for cruisers, adventures bikes, and touring motorcycles, so don’t go thinking about adding your crotch rocket to this one; it needs more torque.
Photo: Sidewinder Sidecar Campers What we don’t know just yet is the GVWR of this unit, or any other of the Sidewinder options, but it can’t be very much considering the strain this beast will already place on your engine.
Sure, it’s not for everyone, especially since some folks are looking for minimal changes to their vehicle and prefer a towable camper, but there are clearly some people out there that can see the value in modifying their motorcycle to adopt such a beast.
As for pricing, the manufacturer’s website makes no mention and urges potential owners to reach out to them directly, but the smallest unit from the brand, the Pygmy, starts off at around $10K (€9,000).
I can’t wait to see the next stage in the evolution of motorcycle campers. Maybe we’ll some something special at EICMA 2026; we’ll be heading there in a couple of days from now.

Altera Agilex 27 Target Markets
New generation FPGA announcements do not come often, which makes this a bit exciting for us. Today, Altera is introducing the Agilex 27 as the first family in its new Agilex 2X portfolio. Agilex 27 pairs hardened 800GbE and 1.6TbE Ethernet with PCIe 6.0 and 7.0 support, and offers configurable transceivers up to 256Gbps. What is more exciting, and what I learned on the pre-briefing call, is that Altera also has a new AI-assisted mode for putting these FPGAs to use.
HyperFlow and Third-Generation HyperFlex
A major new feature of the Agilex 27 family is HyperFlow. HyperFlow is a new full-chip distributed data network that Altera says can move data at multi-terabit-per-second rates throughout the FPGA. That traffic runs on a dedicated network instead of the programmable fabric, so it does not consume soft logic resources or add routing congestion. That leaves more FPGA resources for the application. As an example, a 1.6TbE Ethernet port can bring traffic in through hardened I/O, HyperFlow can carry it across the chip, and the soft logic can spend its resources on processing rather than moving data.
Altera Agilex 27 FPGA architecture
The new family has memory controllers for DDR5, LPDDR4, LPDDR5X, and LPDDR6. It also supports UCIe, has crypto acceleration, and Arm Cortex-A720 and Cortex-A520 cores. A trend we have seen in both Altera and Xilinx high-end FPGAs over the past few years is that programmable logic is surrounded by more hardened IP blocks that help bring designs up faster. Ten years ago, the focus was mostly on the programmable logic elements and I/O, but now much more is happening here.
Agilex 27 also carries third-generation HyperFlex registers distributed throughout the routing fabric. Altera says Quartus Prime can re-time and pipeline designs through those registers without consuming logic resources. Altera claims a 1.8X generation-over-generation performance-per-watt improvement over Agilex 7 for HyperFlex in Agilex 27.
Altera Agilex 2X FPGA portfolio
Agilex 27 sits at the high-performance end of the Agilex 2X portfolio, above the mid-range Agilex 25 and the value-optimized Agilex 22 and Agilex 23. Agilex 22 is FPGA-only, while Agilex 23 adds SoC options.
QuartusIQ AI Companion
QuartusIQ is an AI companion for Quartus Prime that helps developers prioritize steps across compile, timing, debug, and verification. In Altera internal benchmarks comparing Quartus Prime with and without QuartusIQ, design creation was up to 10X faster, and the total design cycle was up to 1.5X faster. The tool integrates with MCP and supports a bring-your-own-key setup.
Altera QuartusIQ FPGA development
At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026, the companies announced that this would be coming to the new RTX Station systems (Windows versions of the DGX Station platforms we have been reviewing at STH). The idea is that you can use QuartusIQ and MCP to design and implement workflows on the chip with local NVIDIA Nemotron as the model. I love this.
Final Words
The other bit to know about FPGA announcements is that there is generally a big gap between announcement and availability. I asked on the call, and the QuartusIQ bits are this quarter, and the Agilex 27 engineering samples are expected in the second half of 2027. What I really wanted to know is how long it would take to get Agilex 27 and have a local model via MCP build me something like an RDMA-enabled 1.6TbE NIC. My sense is that it will be a 2027 or 2028 timeframe when that happens. It is also something I am super excited about since a barrier to using FPGAs has always been having to know how to program them. At some point, Altera and Xilinx can expand FPGA use if they can deliver AI tools that abstract the hardware platform further. I have a goal of being able to get an FPGA card and have an AI agent implement a NIC or a firewall from scratch on it without having to really get my hands dirty designing the RTL. One day it will happen, and I guess the timeframe is 2027/2028.

Larry Cothran did not set out to become what he now calls the number one trucking content creator in the world, he set out to post one video a day and then simply refused to stop, and that stubborn daily discipline, showing up on Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube every single day for more than three years without missing once, is what turned a truck driver with a phone into a media brand that by his own count pulled north of five billion views in a single year. His story is worth telling not because the numbers are enormous, though they are, but because of the quieter lesson running underneath it, which is that producing the work turned out to be the easy part and learning what that work is actually worth has been the hard one.
The Barbecue Detour That Doubled As A Marketing Lab
One of Cothran’s most telling ventures did not happen on the road at all but during a stretch when he had stepped off the truck. By his account it began around 2006 with a piece of small-town serendipity, a chance roadside encounter that ended with a pitmaster handing him an entire barbecue operation, grill and concept included, after a divorce pulled the man out of the business. Cothran did not have a building or a recipe, but he had Facebook, and that turned out to be enough. He built the whole thing on social posts, calling out his location in real time and pulling customers to a folding table. The early roadside version got shut down by the health department for operating without permits, a reminder that the hustle was ahead of the paperwork, and he went and took a driving job. But the barbecue kept pulling him back, and by 2015 he and a partner had opened a brick-and-mortar spot in Rome, Georgia that he says he took from ranked number 164 to the number one result on Google, Yelp, TripAdvisor, and Bing in under 90 days, all of it off Facebook. He eventually handed the restaurant to his partner and went back on the road for good, but the instinct that venture revealed, that perception packaged well sells every time, is the same one that would later define his trucking content.
Into The Cab, And Then Onto The Screen
Cothran has been driving since around 2007, starting out at the kind of entry-level carriers most owner-operators remember before settling into the lease arrangement he has held for close to five years. He still runs real miles, around 2,000 a week hauling transformers and oversize freight on lanes that keep him close enough to get back to the house in a day, which is its own quiet philosophy about what over-the-road life should cost a person. The driving never stopped. What changed was that in May 2021 he started talking to a camera.
The first video that moved was a blunt one, a take on the gap between what the public thinks truckers earn and what drivers say they actually make. It landed around 13,000 views, FreightWaves reached out for an interview, and Cothran decided on the spot that trucking was his lane. From there he did the thing almost nobody sustains, posting one video every single day from May 2021 until September 2024 without missing once. He leaned into short, green-screen comedy, the trucker with the Bluetooth headset who takes a sudden phone call mid-conversation, bits built to be recognized and repeated, and several of them detonated. He points to a lion-statue clip that did 25 million views, a seven-second video that reached 164 million, and a news-style post about a highway incident that crossed 20 million views overnight and became, he says, his most lucrative post to date. Totaled up, he counts 5.11 billion views across a recent 365-day stretch, a figure he uses to plant his flag as the most-watched voice in the space.
The follower numbers fill in the rest of the picture. By his own tally he is roughly 3,000 people shy of 1.5 million on Facebook, sits near 497,000 on Instagram across more than 5,000 posts, and carries another 161,000 on TikTok against 6.5 million lifetime likes, with smaller footprints on Threads and Snapchat on top of that. He is deliberate about where that attention lives. Facebook is his house, he says, because it pays the most and holds his largest audience, while Instagram functions more like a mixtape, a channel that may not pay directly but keeps him in front of people so they do not forget he exists. It is a creator thinking like a distributor, matching each platform to a job rather than chasing whichever one is fashionable.
From Creator To Something Like Press
Lately Cothran has drifted from pure comedy toward reporting. He goes to truck stops and asks drivers directly what they are hearing, whether a rumored shutdown is real, how rates feel on the ground, and he has sat down with veterans, including a driver with more than half a century behind the wheel who lived through the 1983 strike. What is notable is his restraint. He says he does not put definitive calls out into the world, he asks questions and lets drivers supply the answers, staying neutral on the hot topics because his role, as he sees it, is to provide the platform rather than to tell people what to think. For a creator whose incentives all push toward hotter takes, that is a discipline worth respecting, and it is part of why his reporting travels.
The Cost Of Being Seen
Visibility on that scale carries a dark side, and Cothran is candid about it. As his reach grew, so did the trolls, and the harassment escalated past insults into inbox threats on his life, with some of the ugliest of it aimed at his family. He traces the real turn to around Easter of 2023, and it spiked again after one of his posts about a highway incident went viral the following year, the same stretch in which he says he earned the most he ever had in a single week. His response was counterintuitive. He stopped reading comments altogether, refused to engage, and let the online anger turn into its own form of traction rather than letting it push him off course. More telling, he answered the hostility with volume. The very window the threats were escalating is the window his output climbed, from the single daily video he had posted for more than three years to five videos a day in September 2024 and then ten a day by January 2025. The man who once admits he cared deeply what people thought decided he no longer would, stopped looking at the comments that used to sting, and poured that energy back into the work. That is the perseverance sitting underneath the view counts, a creator who met death threats and trolls by posting more, not less, and never broke stride.
The Part Nobody Teaches, Which Is What You Are Worth
The thread that kept surfacing in our conversation was value, and specifically how badly people in this industry tend to price themselves. Cothran has lived both sides of it. He was the number one recruiter at a major carrier for three straight years on the strength of links buried in his videos, paid per driver he brought in, and he describes the familiar sting of people walking up to tell him they signed because of him on months when the payouts somehow did not reflect it. That experience taught him to stop leaving his income to someone else’s referral math.
So he raised his prices, deliberately and repeatedly. He started out charging a modest rate for a single video and pushed it upward step by step over the years, climbing steadily into far higher territory, guided by a simple test he picked up along the way, that the right price is the one that makes you smile when you say it. The deeper shift was philosophical. He learned to stop accepting affiliate and link deals, the arrangements where a brand pays a small cut for every customer a creator funnels in while getting permanent access to that creator’s audience. The math, laid out plainly, is lopsided. A brand spending enormous sums on advertising will offer a creator a few dollars per converted customer, as if a direct line to millions of impressions were worth pocket change. The better model, the one he has moved toward, is to charge brands for the privilege of being present inside his community rather than renting out his credibility by the click.
That is also where the unglamorous business infrastructure comes in. Two of the strongest pieces of advice to come out of the sit-down were to put a general counsel on retainer and to never sign a scope of work a real attorney has not read. A friend who happens to be a lawyer is not the same as paid counsel whose job is to protect your interest, and the fine print is where creators get taken, the clauses that quietly dictate how long a video must be, demand that a post stay pinned to your personal page, or otherwise hand a brand control over real estate you own. The same applies to events. A sponsorship is not a favor, it is an investment a brand expects a return on, which means a creator needs a real activation kit that can speak to brand impressions, recirculation, and measurable ROI, not just a price and a promise.
Why He Is Building A Christmas Party
The project Cothran is pouring himself into now is a Christmas party for truckers in the Cartersville, Georgia area, north of Atlanta, and the why behind it says as much about him as the view counts do. He has been to plenty of industry events that feel buttoned-up and built for executives, and he set out to make the opposite, a come-as-you-are night aimed squarely at the driver. The pitch is intentionally unpretentious. Leave the suit that no longer fits at home, show up in jeans with the headset on, and just be yourself. The point is for drivers to eat, dance, let loose, and spend a night in a room full of people who do what they do, without the cost of admission being a dress code or a title.
Underneath the fun is a conviction about relationships that Cothran learned the hard way out on the road. He tells the story of a driver he once helped get on with a carrier who later returned the favor many times over, repeatedly putting Cothran’s name in for bigger oversize loads and, as he puts it, money in his pocket, all because of a single introduction. That, in his telling, is how doors actually open in this business, not through load boards or algorithms but through people who look out for each other, and he wants to build the room where those connections can happen. He is selling tickets now and still lining up sponsors, promoting the event with weekly videos in the run-up, and true to the lesson running through his whole story, it is the kind of event that should be heavily sponsored precisely because of the audience and the visibility he can put behind it.
Why It Matters
Cothran’s rise is a case study in two things the trucking world consistently undervalues, the compounding power of showing up every single day and the hard business discipline of pricing your own work correctly. For the driver, dispatcher, or small operator sitting on a good story and a phone, the takeaway is not that virality is luck but that it rewards relentless consistency, and the warning is that building the audience is only half the job, because the creators and small businesses who get taken advantage of are almost always the ones who never learned to put a real number, and a real contract, on what they bring to the table.
This article is based on a sit-down conversation between FreightWaves Playbook and trucking content creator Larry Cothran. Audience figures, view counts, and earnings are as stated by Cothran. His Christmas party for drivers is planned for the Cartersville, Georgia area.
